brief.head: Age brings judgment
brief.text: Memory, problem-solving and even creativity peak in youth and middle age, Ajay Shah said. Age brings judgment: the spidey sense that a pawn storm is coming. {094-C05}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah read the wise side of Twitter
lead.head: Twelve tweets to live by
body: Amit Varma keeps a folder of tweets he calls Good Gyan. In the second episode built on it, he read twelve to Ajay Shah, and the two talked over what each was worth.
It began with John Coltrane: “You can play a shoestring if you’re sincere.” Varma aimed it at people who say they cannot afford a good guitar, or own only a phone camera. {094-C01}
William Shakespeare, Varma said, did not refuse to write for want of a laptop. “He found a quill from somewhere.”
## Comfort and greatness

Greg Isenberg’s tweet was five words long: greatness and comfort rarely coexist. Varma, who calls himself an extreme introvert, started his podcast anyway, and hated how he looked on camera in the show’s early episodes. “But I just barreled through,” he said. {094-S02}
Shah urged comfort with physical discomfort: dingy hotels, hard travel, bad food. Varma’s caveat: worrying about next month’s rent is a real cognitive burden.

Neither host would fetishise the sprint. The lives of Newton and Einstein, Shah said, were of extreme concentration and focus. You need the din of the world to collect dots, Varma said, and stillness to let them soak in.
## What effort builds
John Collison, a founder of Stripe, wrote that the world is a museum of passion projects. Shah added an old Turkish proverb: a forest takes a hundred years to grow and one night to burn.
Paul Graham’s arithmetic, that most of the best people at anything are born abroad, became a case for international teams. Growth matters, Shah said, because India wastes so many Ramanujans.
Dharmesh’s call to be an imperfectionist drew Varma’s case for a bias for action, and Shah’s condition: ship your genuine best, and learn the principle behind every correction.
The bodybuilder Ronnie Coleman supplied the bluntest line: “Everybody wants to be a bodybuilder, but nobody wants to lift no heavy ass weights.” {#coleman}
Varma used it to separate thin desires, copied from others, from thick ones, loved for the work itself. People with thin desires, he said, won’t put in the hard yards.
## When comfort becomes the problem

Anthony Bourdain wrote of a lazy guy in his head. Varma’s, he confessed, practically dwarfs him. Shah, a self-described junkie, has never felt the conflict. “Find purpose, the rest will follow,” is his motto. {094-C19}

Sahil Bloom’s tweet, that there is no such thing as making it, left Varma worried about complacency, his own included. Shah found it too bleak. The real problem, he said, is short-termism: many of their viewers work hard but take too few risks.
Gurwinder Bhogal warned that the future is constantly shrinking. Shah’s answer to vague angst about the world was to be selfish: ask what you will read, write and do tomorrow.
The last tweet was from Frog and Toad, in which Frog’s father promises that spring is just around the corner. Things get better, Varma said, but only when you do things. {094-C23}
“We each of us have to wake up and do things,” Shah said.

Shah then admitted he had come without his promised seven recommendations, so Varma drafted the crew, who were, he said, “truly beautiful, inside and outside”. “The good Lord put the ugly one in front of the camera.”

second.label: Isaac Newton
second.head: The moon could wait
second.deck: Ajay Shah on why greatness is quiet concentration, not a frantic sprint
body: Isaac Newton, Ajay Shah said, already had pretty much all the right ideas when he made a rough calculation of the moon’s period. It came out about ten or fifteen per cent off. {094-S06}
Newton concluded he was wrong, and sat quietly. Months and years later, better constants reached him, the pieces of the puzzle clicked, and he saw that he had been right all along.

“I would not fetish the sprint,” Shah said, rejecting startup culture’s adrenaline-laced hard work. {#sprint} The lives of Newton and Einstein, he said, were lives of extreme concentration and focus, passionate about perfectionism.

quote.text: Newton concluded, Okay, so I’m wrong. And he sat quietly.

third.head: Master turned bug tester
body: Ajay Shah will point out a kind of mistake to a young colleague once, twice or thrice. By the fifth or sixth time, he wonders if they are even noticing.
Then, he said, he has become somebody’s bug tester: he finds the mistakes in shoddy code or a bad document, and “like a clerical function” they get fixed. No lesson sticks.
He looks for a thirst for excellence: ship your genuine best, and ask of every correction what the general principle is. Otherwise you are a typist fixing a typo.

“Then you have turned your skilled master into your bug tester, which is a waste of life,” Shah said. {094-S09} Amit Varma added that people who use a mentor as a crutch, not a tool, are exactly the kind AI will replace. {094-C16}

p2.title: The gyan folder
p2.deck: Amit Varma keeps many hundreds of tweets in a Good Gyan folder. Twelve made the cut. {#folder}

sections.label: Good Gyan One
sections.head: No Fender, no excuse
sections.caption: playing a shoestring
body: John Coltrane said you can play a shoestring if you’re sincere. Amit Varma loves the line because of the excuses it answers. {094-C01}

People tell him they want to learn the guitar but cannot afford a Fender, or want to start a YouTube show but have only a phone camera, “not even an iPhone”. His reply: none of that matters. William Shakespeare, he said, found a quill from somewhere and got the job done.
Coltrane had earned the intro: the hosts’ friend Shruti Rajagopalan, a huge fan, named her two dogs Cole and Train.
## Learning on air
The hosts’ own show was Varma’s example. Neither of them knew anything about YouTube when they started, he said, “but we jumped into it and I think we did great.”
Ajay Shah, with the show approaching its hundredth episode, said he was “astonished and happy beyond my wildest dreams”. {#youtube}

Conventional mass media, he said, chases volume and does not push this kind of exotic content. Once, the BBC had to commission Jacob Bronowski’s *The Ascent of Man*; now YouTube lets two people build “a lot of timeless material” for “a tiny cadre of crazy people all over the country, all over the world”.

~ Shah later added his own list of excuses to ignore: no invitation to a Rockefeller Foundation castle in Italy, no hundred-dollar pen. You can read and think, he said, on the floor of an Indian second-class train. {094-J02}

quote.text: If you really want to do something, go out there, get the job done.

sections.label: Good Gyan Two
sections.head: Happy in shark waters
sections.caption: comfort and greatness
body: Greg Isenberg’s tweet offered five words: greatness and comfort rarely coexist. {#greatness} Amit Varma felt leaving the comfort zone was worth it, and admitted he did not do it enough.

Ajay Shah’s antidote, in the realm of ideas, is to index every view on a zero-to-one scale of how sure he is, and of whether it came from authorities or his own reasoning. Enter a new field and every value starts near zero, which holds no terror. {094-C02}
Then, he said, you are swimming in shark-infested territory, “and that’s a good place to be”.
## The price of comfort

Varma saw a trade-off. Time, bandwidth and energy are limited, and some things in the comfort zone “we are bloody good at”. If mastering a craft takes ten thousand hours, should three thousand go elsewhere? {#tenhours}

Perhaps greatness is “an alluring false target”, he wondered, which arrives by the way while you live. Shah’s answer was practical: you know greatness only in hindsight. In the flow, all you can observe is your energy, excitement and concentration. {094-C06}
~ Varma also borrowed from Bob Dylan: “He not busy being born is busy dying.” {094-J13}

quote.text: What is worth living for is a life of the mind, is a journey of the mind.

sections.label: Good Gyan Four
sections.head: Grateful for a clear nose
sections.caption: ordinary moments
body: Brene Brown wrote that we chase extraordinary moments instead of being grateful for ordinary ones, until hardship leaves us begging for a normal moment. Amit Varma, who found her words in a tweet by Polina Pompliano, called it beautiful. {094-R16}
He has lived it. When a bad cold blocks a nostril, he thinks of all the days he breathed freely and was not grateful.

On an earlier shoot at the same location, he skipped the usual ten-to-fifteen-minute walk because his chest felt constricted. That was before his heart attack. Now he can come on the walk again. {094-S07}
## Care by calendar

Varma’s word for what matters is intentionality. Tiago Forte’s tweet had listed four kinds of productivity, task, intellectual, emotional and social, and Varma said we are intentional about tasks but rarely about the rest. {#tiago}

Ajay Shah was nervous: friendships should be spontaneous, not calculating. Varma said he meant caring, not transactional. One friend of theirs meets a new person every week, and calls a loved one every single day. {094-C11}
~ Shah, for his part, resisted the word productivity. “Ultimately you need imagination,” he said. {094-C09}

quote.text: Now I can come on the walk. That ordinary moment is so important.

sections.label: Good Gyan Six
sections.head: No quota for genius
sections.caption: talent born abroad
body: Paul Graham’s tweet offered “some very simple math”: if a country has five per cent of the world’s population and ability is evenly distributed, 95 per cent of the best people at anything will be born abroad. Amit Varma read it as an answer to today’s xenophobia. {094-C13}
Ajay Shah’s case in point was Gukesh’s world-championship team, for which Anand helped find a Polish helper and others. “There was no Indian quota,” he said. {094-S08}
Indian firms, he argued, should hire explicitly multinational workforces. Not all knowledge is in India, and the cultural homogeneity of many workplaces is an impediment.
## Wider tails
If you are one in a million, Shah said, there are 1,400 of you in India. The tragedy is how many are wasted: “just think of all the Ramanujans in India who are being wasted”. {094-J17}
Variance, he argued, is cultural as well as biological. A society that embraces mavericks, dissidents and nonconformists gets more people in the upper tail; an obedient one gets a tight distribution.
~ Varma took on the case against low-skilled migrants. They do jobs locals don’t want, he said, and slums are the entry point to the city for many people. {#slums}

quote.text: All the good things in the world come from that handful of upper tails.

sections.label: Good Gyan Seven
sections.head: Imperfect, and proud of it
sections.caption: being an imperfectionist
body: Dharmesh’s tweet said imperfectionists hit publish, ship product and iterate publicly: “They dream big, but iterate small.” Amit Varma called it almost the mantra of his life. {094-R19}

He tells writing students that perfection is the enemy of production. Whatever you start, you suck at first, and you get good only by doing. His advice: own the suckiness. He admits he preaches it more than he practises it: “I should have written ten books by now.”
Ajay Shah said this way of thinking came to him from Varma. He agreed on volume, but wanted every piece shipped as best you know.
## Thinking, not dawdling

Shah confessed to two stages of procrastination. The first, mulling a problem until the pieces click, he no longer counts as procrastination. Varma had a name for it: “The Bengali word for it is marination.” {094-J05}

The second is perfectionist terror of the idea that arrives too late. His fix comes from big software projects, which plot new bugs found per day and ship once the count has held at zero for a couple of days. {#bugcurve}
~ Varma conceded that his own slogan risks a false binary. “Perfection is achieved only through constant production,” he said. {094-C15}

quote.text: At this point I’ve stopped calling it procrastination. I think I was actually thinking.

sections.label: Good Gyan Ten
sections.head: The lion has a freezer
sections.caption: comfort and complacency
body: Sahil Bloom’s tweet told the old story of the savannah: every morning the gazelle must outrun the lion, and the lion the gazelle. There is no such thing as making it, he wrote; Apple must keep making iPhones. {094-R22}

Amit Varma agreed that complacency, a side effect of prosperity, is a great danger. Then he updated the parable: today’s lion can store gazelles in the freezer, and the gazelle can live in a gated society. “Like no one should be eaten.” {094-J08}
Ajay Shah found the tweet “too bleak by half”, a “life is short, nasty, and brutish view of the world”. {094-J18}
## Risk, not grind

Most of us have more space than that, he said. The real choke points are short-termism and chasing likes instead of genuine thought. “I think a lot of EIE viewers are workaholic, but not enough risk is present in their lives and in their worlds.” {094-C20}

Gurwinder Bhogal’s tweet raised the stakes. Varma’s exercise for anyone in their thirties living away from their parents: make an optimistic guess of their lifespan and of how often you will see them each year. The total is not a lot. {#parents}
~ Shah’s advice was to be selfish: you control only what you do, and a very good you creates positive externalities for everyone around you.

quote.text: Your future is constantly shrinking. So the longer you spend preparing for it, the smaller it’s going to be.
quote.who: Gurwinder Bhogal, as read by Amit Varma

side.boxText: The twelve came from Twitter: John Coltrane, Greg Isenberg, Tiago Forte, Brene Brown via Polina Pompliano, John Collison, Paul Graham, Dharmesh, Ronnie Coleman, Anthony Bourdain, Sahil Bloom, Gurwinder Bhogal and Frog and Toad. Amit Varma urged viewers to follow such accounts. {094-R17}

contQuote.text: Spring does not come on its own. Perhaps spring is already there and you just have to look inside your mind to find it. But your actions also matter.

stories.caption: his father and three regrets
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the path his father set
stories.head: A gift from his father
body: Early in the episode, after asking how he felt about their YouTube journey, Amit Varma put a second question to Ajay Shah. Set aside whether he got into a university to study it, or lived in a big city among like-minded people: what would he have done no matter what?

Shah said he did not know how to think about his life without all of its cultural context. He reminded Varma of the “ridiculous ten and a half hour conversation about my life” the two had once recorded. {#tenhalf}
“I feel like I’m just completely tied to that trajectory,” he said. He grew up with his father, and with an interest in the world, “and that was everything”.
His father died when he was seventeen. “But I got that interest in the world from him,” Shah said, “and I don’t know how to think about it any other way.” {#seventeen}
Once that interest was in place, he said, he did not need the luxury of money and resources, books and universities. “I would have just powered and done it.”

Then came a confession. “I have three great regrets in my life,” he said. He does not know how to play a musical instrument. He wishes he knew maths, “really seriously”. And he wishes he knew more biology. {094-S01}
~ Varma did not linger. His next tweet, by Greg Isenberg, was about greatness and comfort, and how rarely the two coexist.
stories.why: Shah’s curiosity, in his telling, was inherited rather than chosen, and once he had it, nothing could have stopped him. Yet even a mind that keeps starting new fields carries a short list of roads not taken.
stories.postscript: Later, Nomsita Haritashya turned his first regret into a recommendation: pick up a musical instrument, if you have even two per cent of the willpower. {094-R12}

stories.start: I feel that that representation is both true and false.
stories.end: And I think that kind of thing is just crazy
stories.caption: the poker grinders
stories.kicker: Amit Varma remembers his professional poker days
stories.head: Fifteen tables and a bottle
body: Nomsita Haritashya, who edits the show, had a question from behind the camera. Pop culture shows greatness as discomfort: long hours, no sleep, a protein bar instead of a meal. How should a young person read that?
Amit Varma said the picture was both true and false. Excellence takes hard work, but burning yourself out is not the only path to greatness.

He remembered his professional poker days. Some players multi-tabled fifteen tables at a time, “and they’d actually keep a bottle with them because they wouldn’t want to get up to go pee”. {094-S05} “I think that kind of thing is just crazy,” he said.
~ His counterweight was Cal Newport’s *Slow Productivity*, which he read on a flight: let ideas marinate in a quiet life. {094-R01}
stories.why: Hard work matters, but grind is not the whole of it. You need the din of the world to collect dots, Varma said, and the stillness of *thehrav* and *sukoon* to let them soak in. {094-C07}

stories.start: Number one, in my case, the bugs never go to zero
stories.end: you did this, or Bhai Yamit, you did that, so that helps
stories.caption: the king of typos
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on publishing, mistakes and all
stories.head: Read twice, then publish
body: Amit Varma calls himself the king of typos. He has written hundreds of columns and, in blogging days that ended fifteen years ago, “literally many thousands of posts”.
Avoiding typos, he said, would be impossible for him. So his method is simple: write, read it over once, read it over twice, and publish.
“And I will always miss a typo,” he said. “But always, always, always. Within a couple of days no typos exist on that page because readers have written to me.” {094-S10}
~ They write to say he did this or did that, “so that helps”. It was his reply to Ajay Shah’s bug curve: in his case, he said, the bugs never go to zero.
stories.why: Shipping and letting readers help with the fixes beats endless private polishing. It is the imperfectionist creed that Varma calls almost the mantra of his life, and preaches to his writing students even when he falls short. {094-R19}

stories.start: You know, uh in an episode with me, Roshan Abbas once pointed out
stories.end: But I'm comfortable. And that comfort kinda worries me.
stories.caption: FU money and FO money
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the risk of feeling comfortable
stories.head: Too comfortable for comfort
body: Sahil Bloom’s tweet, that there is no such thing as making it, sent Amit Varma back to an episode of *The Seen and the Unseen* with Roshan Abbas. {094-R33}
Varma had asked him about FU money and FO money. Abbas said he had FU money, but not FO money. He gave figures for both, Varma recalled, and “they’re both insane”.
“I’m far from both of them,” Varma said. “But I’m comfortable. And that comfort kinda worries me.” {094-S11}
~ Prosperity is incredible, he said, but one of its side effects is complacency: it is not that hard to get prosperous enough to lose the hunger, to feel you have achieved what you set out to.
stories.why: Comfort can quietly dissolve the hunger that earned it, Varma warned. Ajay Shah thought most people have more room than the lion-and-gazelle story allows, and need more risk in their lives rather than more grind.
